question: Why are airplane windows rounded?
script: Airplane windows are rounded because curved edges spread pressure stress more smoothly around an opening than sharp corners. Repeated cabin pressurization creates cycles of load in the fuselage, so designers avoid abrupt corners that concentrate stress. The early de Havilland Comet helped demonstrate how important this is: investigators found high stress concentrations around squarish window and frame corners. Modern passenger windows use rounded shapes and reinforced frames to manage those loads over many flights. The curve is therefore not mainly about the view. It is a structural choice that helps the fuselage handle pressure cycles safely and efficiently. Each flight adds another cycle, and small reductions in local stress can matter over a long service life. That familiar oval shape is a simple-looking example of engineers guiding forces around an opening instead of letting them pile up at a sharp corner.
beats: Early Comet windows taught a major lesson
